Size of equations

Source: R/equation_size.R
equation_size.Rd

Compute the size of equations written in LaTeX, as they are displayed with an OpenType math font.

The equations are converted to MathML with 'KaTeX' (the MathML used by transform_mathjax()), then laid out with the rules of TeX and the constants of the 'MATH' table of the font: spaces between operators, fractions, scripts, limits of large operators, radicals, stretchy delimiters, matrices, accents. Words and spaces have the widths stored in the font file.

The result does not depend on a graphic device or an application, only on the font file. It is close to what 'Microsoft Word' displays with the same font (a few percent on usual equations), see the section "Differences with Word and browsers".

Usage

equation_size(x, font = gdtools::stixmath_file(), size = 12, display = FALSE)

Arguments

x

a character vector of LaTeX math expressions.

font

an OpenType math font, i.e. a font with a 'MATH' table: the path of a font file, or a family name such as "STIX Two Math", "Latin Modern Math", "Libertinus Math" or "Cambria Math", found with 'systemfonts' (fonts registered with systemfonts::register_font() can be used). The default is the file of 'STIX Two Math' shipped with 'gdtools' (gdtools::stixmath_file()): the results are then the same on every machine. Use font = "STIX Two Math" for the version installed on the system, if any.

size

font size in points.

display

if TRUE, use the display style (large operators with limits above and below, larger fractions), otherwise the inline style.

Value

A data.frame with one row per equation and columns width, height (above the baseline) and depth (below the baseline), in inches. Equations using a construct that is not supported give NA values, with a warning.

Differences with Word and browsers

The layout follows the rules of TeX, as 'KaTeX' and LaTeX do. Compared with 'Microsoft Word' displaying the equation in display style with the same font, the median difference of width is about 1% on a set of usual equations. The known differences are:

  • Word spaces binary operators and fractions a little less than TeX: about 0.17 em less around each binary operator (2 points at 12 points, as in a + b), and no space of the null delimiters around fractions (0.12 em on each side). Equations with such operators or fractions are a few percent wider than in Word;

  • some equations are given a little more space than in Word, which is harmless when the size is used to set the width of a column: the height of matrices in parentheses (up to 20%), the width of matrices in brackets (about 9%), the height of names of functions with an exponent, such as \sin^2 x (about 20%), the width of \left( ... \right) around a fraction (up to 15%);

  • the size of scripts is an upper bound: Word rounds it down to a half point and displays equations with scripts up to about 4% narrower; 'Microsoft PowerPoint' does not use the script style glyphs of the font and displays them up to about 12% narrower;

  • Word uses the font 'Cambria Math' unless the document sets another math font: the equations are then about 5% wider;

  • browsers displaying the HTML output of 'KaTeX' use the fonts of 'KaTeX': the sizes differ by about 7%. The environment array is also 1 em wider in browsers (and in LaTeX), which add half the space between columns before its first column and after its last one; Word does not, and neither does this function.

See also

equation_grob() to draw an equation with 'grid'.

Examples

equation_size(c("\\frac{a+b}{c}", "x^2 + \\sqrt{y_i}"))
#>       width    height      depth
#> 1 0.2701833 0.1845333 0.09913333
#> 2 0.6187407 0.1465000 0.06433333
equation_size("\\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i", display = TRUE)
#>       width    height     depth
#> 1 0.3531278 0.2637333 0.1801333
